The Common black hawk (Buteogallus anthracinus) exhibits life-history traits typical of a large, long-lived raptor inhabiting neotropical coastal and riparian zones. Field studies indicate that adult females attain a considerably larger asymptotic body mass than males, with the heaviest recorded females reaching approximately 700 grams [Wwi = approximately 700 grams]. In contrast, adult males are notably smaller, with their ultimate wet weight averaging around 572 grams [Wwi = around 572 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is likely linked to divergent reproductive roles, as the larger females may be better equipped for the energetic demands of egg production and extended incubation. The species is thermally sensitive during critical developmental windows, and many life-history milestones have been assessed under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], which approximates the upper range of ambient temperatures in their breeding habitats, the maximum recorded lifespan has been estimated at 13.5 years [am = 13.5 years], a longevity consistent with other Buteogallus species that face relatively low adult mortality rates in undisturbed mangrove forests and estuaries.

Reproductive timing in this species follows a predictable seasonal schedule influenced by prey availability and thermal regimes. In the thermal conditions typical of their neotropical habitats, estimated at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], young black hawks first breed at approximately 2 years after birth [tR = approximately 2 years after birth], reflecting a relatively delayed onset of breeding compared to smaller accipitrids. This delayed first reproduction is typical of species that invest heavily in extended parental care and require several seasons to acquire the necessary foraging skills and secure a high-quality breeding territory. Puberty, or the attainment of sexual maturity, occurs considerably earlier than actual first reproduction, with gonadal development completing at roughly 140.4 days after hatching [tp = roughly 140.4 days after hatching] when measured at the same thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Following puberty, young birds experience a lengthy sub-adult period during which they refine hunting techniques and establish dominance hierarchies before they can successfully compete for nest sites.

Nesting and early developmental stages are tightly coupled with the thermal environment. Egg incubation and the subsequent hatching process have been studied both in the field and in captive populations. At an incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, defined as the total incubation period from laying to hatching, averages approximately 37 days [ab = approximately 37 days], though natural clutches in the wild often exhibit a broader range of 28 to 32 days depending on microclimatic conditions and nest attentiveness. Once hatched, the nestlings enter a vulnerable phase of rapid growth, relying entirely on parental provisioning. The hatchling wet weight at emergence is modest, with neonates typically recorded at about 63.9 grams [Ww0 = about 63.9 grams] shortly after hatching, a value that accounts for roughly nine percent of the adult female mass and rises dramatically as the chick consumes the protein-rich prey items delivered by both parents. This initial mass is critical in determining early survival prospects, as heavier hatchlings tend to exhibit greater competitive ability during feeding bouts.

Fledging represents a major developmental milestone, as the young must attain sufficient wing muscle and flight feather development to leave the nest successfully. Under environmental conditions approximating 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the typical time since birth at fledging is 46.8 days [tx = 46.8 days]. This relatively rapid fledging period is characteristic of many Buteogallus hawks and enables the juvenile to escape the high predation pressure typical of nest sites. After fledging, the young enter a prolonged post-fledging dependence phase during which they continue to receive food from the adults while gradually refining their own hunting abilities. The behavioral transition from being a completely dependent nestling to an independent juvenile is a critical period where mortality is often highest. The species overall reproductive output is modest, with females typically producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] during the breeding season, with each clutch containing an average of 2.5 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing an average of 2.5 eggs].

Comparative analyses across the genus Buteogallus reveal that the Common black hawk occupies an intermediate position in terms of both body size and life-history pace, lying between the smaller Rufous crab hawk and the larger Great black hawk. The pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with adult females averaging 700 grams [Wwi = 700 grams] compared to 572 grams [Wwi = 572 grams] in males, ranks among the most extreme within the genus and may reflect differential selection pressures linked to territory defense versus egg production. The species demonstrates a relatively high maximum reproductive rate when productivity is expressed as annual egg output, with females estimated to produce a maximum of 2.5 eggs per year, corresponding to a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually] of approximately 2.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2.5 eggs per clutch]. This low fecundity is compensated by extended parental care, high nestling survival, and the substantial longevity of older individuals, which may breed for over a decade. The combination of delayed first reproduction, modest clutch size, and extended lifespan underscores a life-history strategy oriented toward stability and adult survival rather than high annual reproductive output.
